# Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve {#sec-logistic-regression}


## Objectives

::: {.objective-list}
- Convert between a probability, its odds and its log-odds, in both directions,
  without looking up the formula.
- Fit a logistic regression in either language and read an odds ratio off the
  coefficient.
- Produce the predicted probability for one named patient by hand from the
  coefficients, and confirm it with `predict()`.
:::

## Why this, here

@sec-frameworks fitted four classifiers and scored them all with accuracy, which
is a property of a whole test set. No clinician has ever treated a test set. The
object a clinician meets is a single patient with a single number attached, and
for logistic regression that number is a probability — which is why this is the
model the booklet uses to learn classification, long before the more accurate
ones.

Getting from a linear model to a probability needs one idea, and the idea is
arithmetic rather than statistics.

## Probability, odds, log-odds

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
p <- 0.8
odds <- p / (1 - p)
logit <- log(odds)
c(probability = p, odds = odds, log_odds = logit)
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np

p = 0.8
odds = p / (1 - p)
logit = np.log(odds)
{"probability": p, "odds": odds, "log_odds": round(float(logit), 4)}
```
:::

Three names for the same belief, on three different scales.

- A **probability** lives in $[0, 1]$.
- The **odds**, $p/(1-p)$, live in $[0, \infty)$. A probability of 0.8 is odds of
  4, usually said as "four to one on".
- The **log-odds** or **logit**, $\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)$, live on the
  whole real line.

Only the third is a scale a linear model can safely be written on: a linear
predictor is unbounded, and so are the log-odds. That single sentence is the
whole reason logistic regression has the form it does.

$$\operatorname{logit}(p) = \log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$$

and running it backwards gives the logistic (sigmoid) function

$$p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)}}.$$

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## This bit has no language
The two equations above are algebra, so there is no R version and no Python
version of them. Everything below is both. Deriving the second from the first
takes three lines and is the only derivation in today's material; do it once,
on paper, and you will never again be unsure which way round `exp` goes.
:::

## Fit it, in both languages, to the same rows

`data/diabetes.csv` again, all 768 patients, one predictor.
We are not splitting here, and the reason is not laziness: this exercise reads
the shape of a fitted curve and the meaning of a coefficient, neither of which is
a claim about unseen patients. The moment we make such a claim — the next
exercise — the split comes back.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidymodels)

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

fit_glucose <- logistic_reg() |>
  set_engine("glm") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ glucose, data = diabetes)

tidy(fit_glucose)
```

## Python

```{python}
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
y = (diabetes["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
X = diabetes[["glucose"]]

fit_glucose = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, max_iter=1000).fit(X, y)
float(fit_glucose.intercept_[0]), float(fit_glucose.coef_[0][0])
```
:::

Both give an intercept of −5.09536 and a glucose coefficient of 0.035485. They
agree to every digit printed because they are now solving the same problem:
`C=np.inf` switches off the L2 penalty that scikit-learn applies by default, and
which R's `glm` never applies at all (@sec-frameworks).

::: {.callout-warning}
## `C=np.inf`, and what to do if your scikit-learn complains
Older versions of scikit-learn spell the same thing `penalty=None`, and versions
from 1.8 deprecate that spelling in favour of `C=np.inf`. If you leave the
argument out altogether you will get a slightly different, penalised fit and the
two languages will stop agreeing — on this dataset in the fourth decimal place,
on a small one in the first.
:::

The fitted model is therefore

$$\operatorname{logit}\big(P(\text{diabetes} = \text{pos} \mid \text{glucose})\big)
= -5.095 + 0.0355 \times \text{glucose}.$$

## Task 1 — Say the coefficient out loud

A log-odds coefficient is not interpretable as it stands, and 0.0355 per
mg/dL is not a sentence anyone would say. Exponentiating turns it into an odds
ratio, and a 10 mg/dL step is a clinically sensible unit. Produce the odds ratio
for a 10 mg/dL rise in glucose.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
beta_glucose <- coef(fit_glucose$fit)[["glucose"]]
or_10 <- ______(10 * beta_glucose)
check_metric_range(or_10, 1.2, 1.7, "odds ratio per 10 mg/dL")
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
source("checks/checks.R")
beta_glucose <- coef(fit_glucose$fit)[["glucose"]]
or_10 <- exp(10 * beta_glucose)
check_metric_range(or_10, 1.2, 1.7, "odds ratio per 10 mg/dL")
```
:::
:::

## Stuck?
The coefficient is on the log-odds scale and you want the odds scale. One
function undoes a logarithm.
:::

Write the sentence the number supports, in full: *every 10 mg/dL of glucose
multiplies the odds of diabetes by about 1.43*. Then write what it does **not**
support. It is not a risk ratio, it is not an effect of glucose on anything, and
it is not a 43% increase in the probability — which the next task makes
uncomfortably concrete.

## Task 2 — One patient, by hand and by machine

A patient presents with a glucose of 120. Compute their log-odds, odds and
probability from the two coefficients, using nothing but arithmetic. Then ask the
fitted object for the same probability and check the two agree.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
b <- coef(fit_glucose$fit)

log_odds_120 <- b[["(Intercept)"]] + b[["glucose"]] * ______
odds_120     <- exp(log_odds_120)
prob_120     <- 1 / (1 + exp(______))

by_machine <- predict(fit_glucose,
                      new_data = tibble(glucose = 120),
                      type = "prob")$.pred_pos

round(c(log_odds = log_odds_120, odds = odds_120,
        prob = prob_120, by_machine = by_machine), 4)
check_metric_range(prob_120, 0.25, 0.35, "P(pos | glucose = 120)")
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
source("checks/checks.R")
b <- coef(fit_glucose$fit)

log_odds_120 <- b[["(Intercept)"]] + b[["glucose"]] * 120
odds_120     <- exp(log_odds_120)
prob_120     <- 1 / (1 + exp(-log_odds_120))

by_machine <- predict(fit_glucose,
                      new_data = tibble(glucose = 120),
                      type = "prob")$.pred_pos

round(c(log_odds = log_odds_120, odds = odds_120,
        prob = prob_120, by_machine = by_machine), 4)
check_metric_range(prob_120, 0.25, 0.35, "P(pos | glucose = 120)")
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
b0, b1 = fit_glucose.intercept_[0], fit_glucose.coef_[0][0]

log_odds_120 = b0 + b1 * ______
odds_120     = np.exp(log_odds_120)
prob_120     = 1 / (1 + np.exp(______))

by_machine = fit_glucose.predict_proba(pd.DataFrame({"glucose": [120]}))[0, 1]

print(np.round([log_odds_120, odds_120, prob_120, by_machine], 4))
check_metric_range(prob_120, 0.25, 0.35, "P(pos | glucose = 120)")
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
b0, b1 = fit_glucose.intercept_[0], fit_glucose.coef_[0][0]

log_odds_120 = b0 + b1 * 120
odds_120     = np.exp(log_odds_120)
prob_120     = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-log_odds_120))

by_machine = fit_glucose.predict_proba(pd.DataFrame({"glucose": [120]}))[0, 1]

print(np.round([log_odds_120, odds_120, prob_120, by_machine], 4))
check_metric_range(prob_120, 0.25, 0.35, "P(pos | glucose = 120)")
```
:::
:::
:::

The answer is a probability of about 0.302: log-odds −0.837, odds 0.433. Now
compare it with the sentence from Task 1. The odds ratio of 1.43 per 10 mg/dL is
constant for every patient; the change in *probability* for the same 10 mg/dL is
not. Going from 120 to 130 moves the probability by about 8 percentage points;
going from 60 to 70 moves it by about 2. The model is linear in the log-odds and
in nothing else, which is exactly what the sigmoid's shape is telling you.

## Task 3 — Draw the curve over the data

Plot the predicted probability against glucose, with the observed outcomes drawn
at 0 and 1 underneath. This is the plot to have in your head whenever anyone says
"the model predicts diabetes".

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
library(ggplot2)
preds <- predict(fit_glucose, new_data = diabetes, type = "prob") |>
  bind_cols(diabetes) |>
  mutate(observed = if_else(diabetes == "pos", ______, 0))

ggplot(preds, aes(x = glucose)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = observed), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ______), colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Glucose (mg/dL)", y = "Observed class (0/1) and P(pos)")
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
library(ggplot2)
preds <- predict(fit_glucose, new_data = diabetes, type = "prob") |>
  bind_cols(diabetes) |>
  mutate(observed = if_else(diabetes == "pos", 1, 0))

ggplot(preds, aes(x = glucose)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = observed), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .pred_pos), colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Glucose (mg/dL)", y = "Observed class (0/1) and P(pos)")
```
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
In R the probability of the event is the column `predict(type = "prob")` named
after the level you want. In Python `predict_proba` returns one column per
class, in the order given by the estimator's `classes_` attribute — print it
before you choose an index.
:::

Two features of this plot deserve a sentence each. The curve never reaches 0 or
1: at the lowest real glucose in the file, 57 mg/dL, the model still gives 0.044,
and it will not tell you a patient is safe. And there are five points at
`glucose = 0`, which is not a glucose a living patient has; the file codes some
missing values as zeros, which @sec-correlation-missing takes apart.

## Task 4 — Which column did you take?

Half of all logistic regression errors are taking the probability of the wrong
class. There is a check for it, and the reason the check works is worth
knowing: a logistic regression with an intercept, scored on the rows it was
fitted to, produces fitted probabilities whose **mean equals the observed
prevalence** exactly. Take the other column and you get one minus it.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
p_pos <- predict(fit_glucose, new_data = diabetes, type = "prob")$______
check_probabilities(p_pos, prevalence = mean(diabetes$diabetes == "pos"))
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
source("checks/checks.R")
p_pos <- predict(fit_glucose, new_data = diabetes, type = "prob")$.pred_pos
check_probabilities(p_pos, prevalence = mean(diabetes$diabetes == "pos"))
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
print("classes_:", fit_glucose.classes_)
p_pos = fit_glucose.predict_proba(X)[:, ______]
check_probabilities(p_pos, prevalence=float(y.mean()))
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer

```{python}
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
print("classes_:", fit_glucose.classes_)
p_pos = fit_glucose.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
check_probabilities(p_pos, prevalence=float(y.mean()))
```
:::
:::
:::

Run it deliberately wrong once — take `.pred_neg`, or column 0 — and read what
the check says. A check you have never seen fail is a check you do not trust.

## The result that should bother you

The original course notes for this material relevel the outcome so that `pos`
comes first, on the reasonable grounds that `pos` is the event of interest. Do
that, and the coefficient on glucose becomes **negative**, while the predicted
probability of diabetes for every patient stays exactly the same.

```{r}
library(forcats)
relevelled <- diabetes |> mutate(diabetes = fct_relevel(diabetes, "pos"))
fit_relevelled <- logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ glucose, data = relevelled)

round(c(original   = coef(fit_glucose$fit)[["glucose"]],
        relevelled = coef(fit_relevelled$fit)[["glucose"]]), 5)

p_orig <- predict(fit_glucose,    new_data = diabetes,   type = "prob")$.pred_pos
p_relv <- predict(fit_relevelled, new_data = relevelled, type = "prob")$.pred_pos
max(abs(p_orig - p_relv))
```

1. `glm()` models the probability of the **last** level of the factor. With
   levels `neg, pos` it models `pos`, so the coefficient is +0.0355: more
   glucose, more diabetes. Relevel, and the last level is `neg`, so the same
   engine now models the probability of *not* having diabetes and reports
   −0.0355.
2. `parsnip` knows this. It asks the engine for its own event, then returns both
   columns correctly labelled, which is why `.pred_pos` is identical to fifteen
   decimal places either way.
3. So the coefficient's sign and the column's name follow two different
   conventions, and the published page that made this change kept a sentence
   underneath saying the model was $\operatorname{logit}(P(\text{pos})) = \beta_0
   + \beta_1 x$. With `pos` relevelled first, that sentence was false and the
   plot above it was right.

The transferable rule: **never read a sign off a coefficient without checking
which class the engine thinks it is modelling.** The cheap way to check is the
one you already have — predict for a patient with a high glucose and see which
direction the probability went.

## Reflection

1. The odds ratio is constant and the probability difference is not. Which of
   the two would you put in a patient-facing leaflet, and what would you have to
   add to make it honest?
2. This model has an accuracy you have not computed and a probability for every
   patient that you have. Which of those two would change if the study had
   recruited twice as many `pos` patients, and why does that matter for a model
   fitted on a case-control sample?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Expected values.** Intercept ≈ −5.10, glucose ≈ 0.0355 (both languages, to
five decimals). Odds ratio per 10 mg/dL ≈ 1.43 (range 1.2–1.7 in the check
allows for regenerated data). At glucose 120: log-odds ≈ −0.84, odds ≈ 0.43,
probability ≈ 0.302. Prevalence 280/768 = 0.365, which is also the mean fitted
probability, exactly.

**Answers.** (1) The odds ratio is stable but means nothing to a patient; the
probability difference is meaningful but depends on where the patient starts.
The honest leaflet gives absolute risks at named glucose values. (2) The
probabilities would change and the odds ratio would not — the intercept absorbs
the sampling fraction. This is why case-control studies can report odds ratios
and cannot report risks, and it is the main reason a model that looks calibrated
in development is not calibrated in the clinic.

**Common failures.** (1) `exp(beta)` reported as a probability. Ask for the
units. (2) In Python, `predict_proba(...)[0]` instead of `[0, 1]` — it returns
both columns and the subsequent check fails informatively. (3) Writing
`predict(fit, new_data = 120)`: parsnip wants a data frame with the predictor's
name, which is strict and correct, and students find it rude.

**Timing.** Task 2 is the one to protect. Task 3 can be done from the front;
Task 4 takes four minutes and prevents a day of confusion in @sec-thresholds.
:::
:::

## Stretch

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 1 — Where is the curve steepest?
Find the glucose value at which the predicted probability is 0.5, from the two
coefficients alone: it is $-\beta_0/\beta_1$. Ours is about 144 mg/dL. This is
the point at which the model is least sure, and — as @sec-thresholds will show —
it is also exactly what you are choosing when you choose a threshold of 0.5.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — Add a predictor, and watch the coefficient move
Refit with `diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age`. The glucose coefficient
changes a little (0.0355 to about 0.0328) and the intercept moves a long way
(−5.10 to about −6.74). Explain why the
second of those is arithmetic rather than news, and what the first one would
have to look like before you called glucose confounded by age.
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that for a patient drawn from this population, the model gives a
probability of diabetes, and that you can produce and interpret that probability
on all three scales.

**Cannot:** that any patient *has* diabetes. The model has not said so and
cannot: a probability is not a decision, and nothing in the fitting procedure
knows what it costs to be wrong in either direction. Turning 0.302 into a yes or
a no is a separate act with separate consequences, and it is @sec-thresholds.
